finding: Test 11 mandates the exact fence §3 rejects, in the same release, so the two sections cannot both be satisfied. §3 decides value scoping this round and states it twice: "`blocking` is refused on every write path; `all` is not. The fence is scoped to the *value*, not to a transition and not to the field", and "A *field*-scoped fence is wider than the argument for it: `all` is the built-in default and the only value that tightens the gate, so refusing it buys nothing and costs a run-halting escalation". Test 11 still reads "Each of `tp set --workflow`, `tp set --workflow --project` and `tp import` exits 2 under `TP_UNATTENDED=1` for both `all` and `blocking`, and 0 without it" -- byte-identical to round 8's wording (verified against snapshot-round-8.md line 195 vs snapshot-round-9.md line 257). An implementation that satisfies test 11 is field-scoped and therefore violates §3; an implementation that satisfies §3 reddens test 11 on three of its six assertions. This is not merely an ambiguity: it is the one input on which the release's central decision this round turns, and §7 is where the implementer gets acceptance from.
suggestion: Rewrite test 11 to the value-scoped fence and keep the two-sinks discipline: under `TP_UNATTENDED=1`, each of the three write paths exits 2 for `blocking`; each of the three exits 0 for `all` and writes it; without `TP_UNATTENDED` all six exit 0. Name the killing mutation explicitly -- a fence keyed on the field name rather than on the value, which is the cheapest branch to add and passes today's wording.

finding: §1 and §4 now give opposite answers to when `by_severity` is emitted, so test 13's word "Present" has no determinate meaning. §1 deliverable 3, unchanged this round: "Emitted unconditionally, so it is the one part every project sees." §4, rewritten this round: "**Emitted when the round has at least one non-`PASS` row, and it survives `--compact`**" -- and it argues the conditionality is load-bearing ("Emitting unconditionally would discard that signal and put the key on every merge of every default-`all` project, which is the case the twin excludes by name"). The two readings differ on an input every project produces: a merge of a round with zero non-`PASS` rows. One engineer asserts `by_severity: {}` is present; the other asserts the key is absent; both cite this spec. §1 is also where an implementer sizes the blast radius, and under §4 the claim that this is "the one part every project sees" is false -- a project whose rounds are clean never sees it.
suggestion: Reword §1's third deliverable to §4's decision in the same breath as the value: the breakdown a project sees on any round that carried non-`PASS` rows, absent when nothing was graded. Then §4 and §7 test 13 can be read together without a contradiction, and the "one part every project sees" claim goes with it.

finding: §4's emission became conditional this round and test 13 did not follow, so the new rule has no test and its killing mutation survives. Test 13 reads in full: "**`by_severity` on `--merge`.** Present, correct over a mixed round, and still present under `--compact`." Every arm is a positive presence arm over a round that has non-`PASS` rows -- exactly the population §4's condition does not discriminate. The mutation that §4 exists to exclude, unconditional emission (an empty map on every merge of every default-`all` project), passes all three arms. Measured on this repository's audit corpus, 90 recorded round files hold 10,435 rows of which only 360 are non-`PASS`, so the majority of real merges are the case with no test.
suggestion: Add the absence arm and name its mutation: a `--merge` of a round whose rows are all `PASS` must emit no `by_severity` key at all (not `{}`, not `null`), and the killing mutation is assigning the counter outside the has-non-PASS-rows guard. Keep the two arms test 13 already has, and pin "correct over a mixed round" to an exact expected map rather than to the word correct.

finding: §4 now names four input shapes for an ungraded severity and test 8 fixtures three, so the shape §4 added this round is the one the fail-closed predicate is never tested on. §4: "A severity that is JSON `null`, absent, or not a string at all keys on **`unrecognised`**" -- and it says why the fourth matters: "`\"\"` is not a bucket: it is what a naive type assertion produces for three different shapes, and it is the hiding this section exists to prevent." Test 8 still reads "three fixtures, for a severity outside the enum, `null`, and absent." The missing shape is the one where the naive Go implementation (`row["severity"].(string)`) and the correct one differ observably, and nothing rejects a non-string `severity` on the audit path. Measured: all 360 non-`PASS` rows in this repository's 90 recorded audit-round files carry a string severity (warning 158, info 109, low 36, error 26, high 16, medium 15), so the corpus supplies no instance of `null`, absent or non-string at all -- every one of test 8's fixtures has to be synthesised, and there is no reason to synthesise three rather than four.
suggestion: Make test 8 four fixtures: a severity outside the enum, JSON `null`, absent, and a non-string (`3` and/or `true`). Correct the trailing sentence at the same time: "A legacy row supplies only the first" is right, but it now reads as if the enumeration were complete at three.

finding: §2 states a required behaviour change to `next_action` on both audit sinks, says "That is part of this release", and §7 has no test for it -- nor does §1's deliverable list carry it. The clause: "Under `blocking` the first clean round of a streak that still holds `warning`/`info` rows changes branch, and the recommendation must name the accepted rows rather than report an empty round." Two defects for a test writer. (a) No observable is pinned: "must name the accepted rows" fixes no field, no key and no string, so one engineer asserts a count in `next_action.reason`, another asserts a new key, another asserts the existing command string is unchanged -- all three satisfy the sentence and only one can match an implementation. (b) No test in the list of fourteen mentions `next_action`, so an implementation that leaves both sinks exactly as they are today ships green: `clean: true` under `blocking` simply routes to the advance-the-phase branch and reports an empty round, which is the failure the clause names. `next_action` survives `--compact` and is the field the loop's driver branches on, so this is the release's most agent-visible behaviour change and its least tested.
suggestion: Either pin the observable and add a test -- a round clean under `blocking` with `warning`/`info` rows open emits `next_action` whose <named field> carries the non-blocking count, asserted on both `--record` and `--status`, killing mutation being today's code unchanged -- or move the clause to §6 as deferred. Do not leave a stated deliverable with neither a pinned observable nor an acceptance.

finding: §2 added the symmetric-stamping paragraph this round and called the relaxing direction "the one to state"; test 9 still tests only the tightening direction, and a concrete implementation passes test 9 while violating the new paragraph. §2: "A round recorded under `blocking` keeps `clean: true` after the knob returns to `all`, so one operator-approved round of `blocking` relaxes that cycle's streak permanently." Test 9 records under `all`, switches to `blocking`, and asserts stored verdicts unchanged. The mutation that separates them is not the live re-grade test 9 already names but a policy FLOOR at the read side -- treat a stored `clean: true` round as unclean when the currently resolved policy is `all` and the round's stored `findings` is non-zero. That is the defensive thing an implementer reaches for ("do not trust a verdict recorded under a laxer policy"), it leaves test 9 green in both of its halves because `all` -> `blocking` only ever relaxes, and it makes §2's stated permanence false and §3's whole write-not-read fence argument moot. This is the half of round 8's repair that did not land: §2 gained the prose, §7 gained nothing.
suggestion: Add test 9's second half with its own killing mutation: record a round under `blocking` that carries `warning`/`info` rows and no `error`, set the field back to `all` without re-recording, and assert that round's `clean`, the cycle's `consecutive_clean` and `converged` are all unchanged on `--status` and on a `--record` of an unchanged results file. Name the mutation as a read-side policy floor, not the live re-grade, since the live re-grade is already named for the other direction.

finding: Test 14's repaired count is arithmetically right and still passes against the mutation it was repaired to catch. Counted against the tree: `TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate` (internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:469-503) contains exactly eleven assert/require call sites, and exactly two of them -- `assert.NotEqual(t, 0, code, "audit_converge_on is not a workflow field")` and `assert.Contains(t, stdout+stderr, "unknown workflow field: audit_converge_on")` -- are the pair §6a reverses, so eleven, two and nine all verify. But "All **nine** surviving assertions of the gate guard still pass" is satisfied by DELETING lines 472-474 rather than flipping their expectations: the guard then holds nine assertions, all nine pass, and the file no longer exercises `audit_converge_on` anywhere. That is the same delete-instead-of-update hazard the draft anticipates for the seven-deletion case and does not close for the two-deletion case, and it is the cheaper of the two edits. Related and unstated: reversing the pair makes the `tp set --workflow --project audit_converge_on=blocking` at line 472 SUCCEED, so assertions 3-11 then execute with the project resolved to `blocking` -- they survive only because `signalRow` (audit_signal_test.go:40-42) emits no `severity` key and §2's fail-closed rule therefore keeps the disposed FAIL blocking at line 490. Nothing in §7 pins that precondition, so a later `severity` added to the fixture helper reddens the guard for a reason unrelated to this release.
suggestion: State the positive form: the gate guard still carries ELEVEN assertions, two of them with reversed expectations -- the `tp set --workflow --project audit_converge_on=blocking` write now exits 0 and its output does not contain "unknown workflow field" -- and the remaining nine pass unchanged. Add the fixture precondition as an assertion in the test rather than as prose: the disposed row carries no `severity`, so it is blocking under both values of the field.

finding: §4's two keying rules collide on one input and the collision is the hiding §4 exists to prevent. Rule one: "A severity that is a string outside the enum keys on that string." Rule two: "A severity that is JSON `null`, absent, or not a string at all keys on **`unrecognised`**." A row carrying the literal string `"unrecognised"` is outside the enum, so rule one keys it on `unrecognised` -- the same bucket rule two owns. The merged count is then unreadable in exactly the way §4 forbids ("Every row lands in a named bucket, because the point is that nothing hides"): an agent reading `{"unrecognised": 3}` cannot tell three ungraded rows from three rows an auditor deliberately labelled `unrecognised`, and the two have different remedies. Measured, the corpus supplies no instance -- the 360 non-`PASS` rows across 90 recorded audit-round files carry only warning/info/low/error/high/medium -- so like the non-string case this will first appear in the field, and test 13's fixture as described would not contain it either.
suggestion: Either pick a bucket name that cannot be a self-declared severity (a key no auditor would write, or a reserved form) and say so as the reason, or state the precedence explicitly -- a literal `"unrecognised"` string keys on itself and the ungraded bucket is named `<something else>` -- and add the colliding row to test 13's fixture so the choice is asserted rather than assumed.
